name: Uma Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Uma. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech firms, employers or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play guitar and sing in a folk and country duo with my cousin Samir. We do Friday nights at the Plough, a family-run pub, and the Saturday farmers' market in summer. In the week I record beginner guitar lessons for my online channel, and I write little jingles for local businesses, like the farm shop and the tyre garage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love building something of my own. The channel has about 2,000 subscribers and pays maybe 120 pounds a month, plus a few people pay for one-to-one video lessons. I use AI every day for editing, captions and planning posts. The hard part is that I'm still a fairly basic guitarist, and money's tight. I'm married to Yusuf, a joiner in his dad's workshop, and we have less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a useful tool and nothing more, and hard work still wins. I'd probably make a video about how I use it to edit my lessons, because people ask. Mostly I'd get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me. I already use AI to save hours on editing, and if it stays at that level, I've got an edge over teachers who don't. My worry is money in general, because we've got no cushion and the pub could close any year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post two lessons a week instead of one and start a paid beginner course for 25 pounds. I'd pitch jingles to three more businesses on the high street. I'd try to save 100 pounds a month so we have a proper cushion before we think about children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly positive, with the usual money nerves underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pub could close. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The man who owns the pub is 66 and his kids don't want the place, so if he sells, my Friday nights become flats. It might happen any year. That's Friday nights gone, about 80 pounds a week for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Yusuf think about your channel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Yusuf thinks it's brilliant, but he'd like it to pay more than his Saturday overtime. Fair enough. I told him give me a year.

She'd make a video on how she **edits lessons** with AI.
think: AI at this level gives her **an edge** over teachers who don't use it.
Her worry is **no cushion** and the pub possibly closing.
do: Post **two lessons** a week and launch a **25-pound** course.
Pitch **jingles** to three more high street businesses.
Save **100 pounds** a month before thinking about children.

Save 100 pounds a month before starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who adapt will be fine, and I plan to adapt. I'd keep it upbeat online, because nobody wants a moaning guitar teacher. I'd also say live music in a pub still needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my online lessons are in trouble. If an AI tutor can watch a beginner through their phone and correct their chords, why buy my videos? The jingles too, a business can type what it wants and get one. What's safest is the duo at the pub and market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my effort into live and local: more pub gigs, weddings with Samir, and in-person group lessons at the village hall. I'd use AI to run the admin, bookings, invoices and posts, so I spend my time playing. I'd sell the channel's course while it still sells, then stop pouring hours into videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit rattled, but up for it. I'd rather change early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should deal with the fallout, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and communities first, honestly. I don't want a handout, I want to be useful. If the council wants to help, give small businesses cheap rent on the village hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're moving away from the channel you've built. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, because it's mine. But twelve people in a village hall paying 8 pounds each beats 2,000 subscribers paying nothing. That's just sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, and families and towns that pull together will get through it. Online I'd share what I'm doing, not what I'm scared of. I wouldn't wait for the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 my channel and jingles are worth nothing, because that's all screen work. The pub and market duo last until robots, around 2031, if the pub's still open. Yusuf's joinery is hands-on too, so our household has maybe three years before the robots reach both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd ask Yusuf's dad if I can learn the workshop side: finishing, varnishing, fitting. That's hands-on and it's family. I'd keep the duo going on weekends. We'd put off trying for a baby for a year or two, which would break my mum's heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. Not panicking, because I'd have a plan by the weekend, but shaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots about three years after the thinking AI, how do you use those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a hands-on trade properly and save every penny from gigs. A joinery workshop with three of us in it might last longer than one guitar teacher. Three years is short, but it's not nothing if you start on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that we're waiting so the baby has a steady home, not a worried one. She'd say her generation never waited for anything. She's not wrong, but she also didn't have AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse to sit still. I'd make videos for other musicians about switching to local, live work. I'd keep the tone hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build something solid. I'd grow the village hall lessons and weddings, and slowly learn the workshop side. The online stuff fades, but I'd squeeze it while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd run two village hall classes a week and book ten weddings with Samir. I'd buy a decent PA second-hand, around 500 pounds, so we can do bigger rooms. I'd spend one day a week at the workshop learning finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and quite hopeful. Worried about money, but it feels like a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a PA with almost no savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the course sales over the winter, probably. I'd only buy a PA once three weddings were booked with deposits, because I'm not borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still start a family on time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a year later than we'd planned, not two. Five years gives us room. My mum would be happier with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work, so get on with it. I'd tell young musicians to learn a trade and a business as well as an instrument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I could build a proper live and teaching business and start a family on time. The pub might close before AGI does, so the next few years still have their own worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the channel going but shift more time to in-person classes and weddings. I'd use AI to automate the admin completely. We'd start saving for a house deposit with Yusuf, slowly, and try for a baby next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's always the money nag, but this one feels like a fair race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get comfortable and keep making videos for too long because they still pay a bit. I'd have to be honest with myself each year about what's growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in place by the time AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full diary of live work, a few regular group classes and a bit of joinery under my belt. And a child at school, hopefully. That's the dream.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Yusuf's work and mine both go within a few years, just when we want a family. What would help is cheap rent on community spaces for small teachers like me, and apprenticeships that let a 27-year-old learn a trade without losing a year's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. A lot of us will survive by working with our relatives. That's not a government scheme, but it's real.
